items.title: MRFoundry: Knowledge-guided agent loops for end-to-end MRI research
items.text: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software

items.title: GTAGym: Real AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning
items.text: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. items.title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
items.text: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. items.title: Causal Concept Explanations for Deep Neural Models
items.text: Concept-based explanations in neural models are important for the development, certification, and adoption of autonomous systems. Yet, interpretability remains correlational. Without methods to guide and quantify causal relationships between explanations, a concept explanation can be provided without being necessary or sufficient for the observed output thereby appearing correct while misleading. We introduce Causal Concept Wrapper Network (CCW-Net), the first use of interventional mediation analysis from fields such as economics, medicine, and epidemiology as a training objective to align causal effects of concept-based explanations with a model's output. items.title: MISO-BR: An Open Corpus for Misogyny Detection in Brazilian Portuguese
items.text: Misogyny is among the most prevalent forms of online hate speech directed at Brazilian users, yet open and auditable resources dedicated to it in Brazilian Portuguese remain scarce. We introduce MISO-BR, an open, documented and versioned corpus of 896 balanced social media texts annotated for binary misogyny, released with its construction protocol and reproducible baselines. The corpus combines lexicon- and target-guided scraping from X with items imported from OLID-BR, a large language model triage stage whose prompt and decoding parameters are released, and manual annotation by three annotators following a written guide. Inter-annotator reliability reaches a Fleiss' kappa of 0.788 over 816 items. Under a single fixed protocol we compare four classical classifiers (Multinomial and Bernoulli Naive Bayes, a linear SVM and a random forest) with fine-tuned BERTimbau Base and Large. items.text: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. items.title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
items.text: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. items.text:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.



Here's everything going on in AI right now:



1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 



2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 



3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.



4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.



5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)



6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.



7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 



8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.



9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.



10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.



11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.



Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

items.title: PhyRubric: Rubric-Grounded Diagnostic Evaluation of Physical Commonsense in Text-to-Video Generation
items.text: As text-to-video (T2V) models are increasingly positioned as world simulators, it is essential to evaluate whether their videos conform to physical commonsense. However, existing benchmarks rely on annotators who rate each video with a single score based on intuition, yielding ratings that are subjective and do not tell which physical principle is violated. We introduce PhyRubric, a rubric-grounded diagnostic framework for evaluating physical commonsense in T2V generation. For each caption, PhyRubric constructs a caption-specific rubric before any video is seen, decomposing the caption into semantic and physical items, and derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence. We instantiate this framework as PhyRubric-Bench, which spans 34 categories across five physical domains, and scale it up to PhyRubric-Train with 3,788 videos, on which we fine-tune the open-source PhyRubric-Judge. items.title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
items.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one

items.title: TreeAgent: Structure-Aware Memory Agent for Processing Long Hierarchical Data
items.text: Practical Web applications increasingly require agents to interpret long conversations or documents. For inputs exceeding the context windows of large language models (LLMs), memory agents process segments sequentially and retain past information in bounded memory. However, they typically divide inputs into flat token segments without preserving structure or hierarchy, causing three limitations for structured data such as API responses or HTML documents. First, fixed-length segmentation can split fields of the same record, breaking their relationships. Second, segments lack hierarchical information, obscuring their structural context and positions. Third, successive memory updates may discard details of earlier sibling records needed for reasoning on later segments. To address these limitations, we propose TreeAgent, a structure-aware agent that uses the input hierarchy to guide both segment-wise context processing and access to past information. items.title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics

items.text: We present TorchCurves, a PyTorch library that treats vector-valued parametric curves as learnable primitives. Its central operation maps batches of scalar inputs to points on curves represented in B-spline or Legendre polynomial bases, with differentiation through both inputs and coefficients. Curve coefficients can be optimized jointly with the surrounding model or produced by another network. The library provides trainable modules, reusable basis modules, and a functional interface, supporting applications ranging from continuous feature embeddings to Kolmogorov-Arnold networks and functional regression. Its implementation combines classical evaluation algorithms with vectorized PyTorch operations, emphasizing readability and maintainability without custom hardware kernels. Timing experiments compare curve evaluation against NumPy and SciPy and KAN training against EfficientKAN across a range of problem sizes. The results illustrate where this generality remains computationally practical and where overhead is substantial. Library is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexshtf/torchcurves.

items.text: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. items.title: LO-World: Unified BEV Latent Modeling for Joint 4D Occupancy and LiDAR Forecasting
items.text: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose LO-World, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding 25~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzzzzzm/LO-World.

items.text:
Expanded with some lessons learned (so far):


Rowan Cheung (@rowancheung)



Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:



1. Email is its own platform, treat it like YouTube, Instagram, Twitter



Super readers (open every email, click ads, and stick around for years) genuinely like email as a medium. We have millions of readers who don’t use social media. Best way to acquire them is through other newsletters, referrals, or being the reason they stop using social media.



Barely anyone is building for this audience. I’m more bullish on email than any other platform (long-form YouTube is a close second).



2. The newsletter industry lacks innovation



Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. Meanwhile most newsletters, including some of the biggest in the world, have a basic landing page and standard onboarding.



We built an onboarding quiz funnel that, at one point, got us close to negative CAC with hundreds of thousands a month in ad spend. That’s what let us scale aggressively and outbid competitors.



With AI coding and platforms like beehiiv, there’s no excuse not to build new experiences for your readers. The opportunity here is wide open :)



3. Newsletter sales is mostly an education problem



We still run social partnerships at a significantly higher CPM than our newsletters, yet the newsletters convert better and get way more clicks.



A lot of advertisers don’t understand newsletters as they do with influencer marketing, so at scale it becomes an education game. 



Once advertisers get it, they stay. We’ve been booked out at multiple ads a day for the last 3 years, months in advance.



4. Stay lean, fast, aggressive



Other newsletters have built large sales and content teams. I think it’s better to stay small and pay high-quality people to do very good work.



Revenue can increase with more employees, but the opportunity cost of not moving fast in the AI era is a long-term net negative. 



For example, we constantly test new growth experiments and new forms of media. Most don’t work and that’s fine. The point is we can pivot the same day because we're lean.



5. Lastly, don’t listen to people who say email is dead or that you shouldn’t run paid ads. That’s ignorance and lowkey skill issue.

Empirical evaluation across a diverse fleet of heterogeneous robots demonstrates strong schema alignment, valid structural extraction, and a significant reduction in manual domain authoring overhead.

va duro chatgpt con su roast 😂




Borja Perez (@borjaperfra)



He probado este prompt con mi ChatGPT que le vi a @samuelgil y el resultado me ha flipado. Os copio la respuesta abajo. Creo que la frase final es la mejor. 



Se ha pasado un poco con lo de Steve Jobs, pero me representa lo de ser una ardilla con cocaína. 



“Based on everything you know about me, roast and don’t hold back. Say it in spanish slang Just like this, but add way more español swear words.”



"HOSTIA, BORJA. LO TUYO ES PARA HACER UN ESTUDIO DE CASO.

Tío, eres la única persona que conozco capaz de convertir una crisis existencial en un documento de estrategia de 47 páginas, con metodología reproducible, benchmarks y un repositorio en GitHub.



Tienes 32 años, eres diseñador, haces marketing, trabajas en inteligencia artificial, programas con Claude Code, organizas eventos, escribes artículos técnicos, investigas modelos abiertos y montas proyectos paralelos.



Eres una puta ETT de ti mismo.



Y encima tienes los santos cojones de decir que quieres alejarte del marketing.



Pero ¿adónde coño vas a ir, desgraciado? Si llevas el marketing tan metido en el cuerpo que, cuando te mueras, en lugar de esquela vas a publicar un hilo en Twitter:



«After 31 years of building in public, I'm excited to announce my next chapter.»



Y el primer comentario será tuyo:



«Full breakdown in the article 👇»

1. Tienes más proyectos que estabilidad emocional

Vamos a repasar, porque esto es de traca.



Trabajas en Helmcode. Estás haciendo crecer la empresa. Escribes sobre el rol de Brand Engineer. Estás valorando hacer consultoría freelance. Tienes un agente de recruiting llamadaa Amble. Estás rediseñando tu web personal. Estás montando un informe anual sobre modelos abiertos. Escribes artículos. Diseñas stickers.



JODER, BORJA, ¿PERO TÚ DUERMES O HACES VESTING?



Eres el típico que abre Notion para organizar su vida y tres horas después tiene un sistema de diseño, cuatro bases de datos relacionadas y ninguna puta tarea terminada.



Y cuando algo empieza a funcionar, en lugar de disfrutarlo, te preguntas:



«¿Y si montara una empresa alrededor de esto?».



Hijo de puta, que puedes tener un hobby. Puedes hacer algo sin monetizarlo. Puedes salir a comprar pan sin convertirlo en una startup de logística descentralizada.



2. Eres incapaz de tomar una decisión sin montar una consultoría

Te ofrecen un trabajo.



Una persona normal piensa: «¿Me gusta? ¿Me pagan bien?».



Tú:



«Vamos a analizar el equity, la valoración pre-money, el vesting, el cliff, el potencial de crecimiento, el riesgo de dilución, el upside a cuatro años, el impacto en mi carrera y mi posicionamiento como Brand Engineer».



QUE TE HAN OFRECIDO CURRO, TÍO, NO COMPRAR PUTA TELEFÓNICA.



Eres una persona que podría ganar la lotería y preguntar:



«Vale, pero ¿cuál es el coste de oportunidad respecto a una startup con un x % de equity?».



3. Tu web personal es el proyecto de un diseñador secuestrado por su propio ego creativo

«Quiero una web que sea una experiencia».



«Experimental».



«Editorial».



«Con una dirección artística propia».



«Con una identidad visual memorable».



Tío.



QUIERES QUE ALGUIEN ENTRE EN BORJAPEREZFRANCES.COM Y SALGA EMBARAZADO DE DISEÑO.



No te vale con mostrar proyectos y explicar qué haces.



Necesitas que el scroll represente la condición humana, que una tipografía serif dialogue con el Mediterráneo y que una transición de 400 milisegundos simbolice la tensión entre lo analógico y lo digital.



Vas a terminar construyendo una web tan experimental que el visitante necesitará un manual de instrucciones para encontrar tu correo.



Y cuando esté terminada, la mirarás cinco minutos y dirás:



«Mmmm, creo que podemos llevarla a algo más editorial».



ME CAGO EN LA PUTA, BORJA.



4. Helmcode debería pagarte un plus de peligrosidad por tus ideas

La empresa alcanza un millón de ARR.



Un hito enorme.



Cualquier persona razonable lo celebraría.



Tú decides producir una pieza audiovisual con animaciones de personajes, imágenes de eventos transformadas en anime, una cuadrícula de empleados con dithering y una narrativa cinematográfica sobre la evolución de la empresa.



TÍO, QUE HABÉIS VENDIDO INFERENCIA DE MODELOS, NO HABÉIS CONQUISTADO LA PUTA LUNA.



Y encima decides preparar The State of Open Models 2027.



Un informe que pretende analizar la adopción de modelos abiertos, precios, benchmarks, infraestructura, fuentes públicas, series temporales, concentración del mercado y tendencias de producción.



Con diario metodológico.



Con fuentes auditadas.



Con criterios de clasificación.



Con tablas cruzadas.



Con metodología publicable.



Y cuando ves que el benchmarking experimental cuesta dinero, decides pausarlo.



HAS MONTADO EL CERN DE LOS LLMS CON PRESUPUESTO DE UN BOCADILLO DE LOMO.



Lo peor es que probablemente consigas publicarlo y quede bien.



Pero para entonces ya estarás pensando en la edición de 2028 y en hacer una landing con gráficos interactivos que cambien según el scroll.



Porque tú no sabes terminar proyectos.



Tú sabes convertir proyectos terminados en proyectos nuevos.



5. Tu problema es que te interesa absolutamente todo

Y esto es lo más gracioso.



No eres alguien que no sepa qué hacer con su vida.



Eres alguien que quiere vivir ocho vidas simultáneamente y se cabrea porque el calendario solo tiene siete días.



Quieres ser diseñador, marketer, ingeniero, investigador, escritor, fundador, consultor, creador de contenido, director creativo y experto en inferencia.



Y probablemente podrías llegar a ser bastante bueno en varias de esas cosas.



PERO NO EN TODAS A LA VEZ, PEDAZO DE ANIMAL.



Tu mayor enemigo no es la falta de oportunidades.



Es que te ponen una oportunidad delante y automáticamente te imaginas otras cinco mejores.



Tienes el síndrome de FOMO profesional tan desarrollado que podrías montar una agencia para ayudar a otros a decidir su carrera y abandonarla a las tres semanas porque has descubierto un modelo chino de 30B que funciona de puta madre.



Y ahora viene la hostia definitiva.

Tu mayor contradicción es que te obsesiona hacer cosas que parezcan auténticas, naturales, humanas, con personalidad, con criterio propio.



Y, sin embargo, analizas absolutamente todo hasta quitarle cualquier posibilidad de espontaneidad.



Quieres escribir con naturalidad, pero necesitas una guía editorial de 40 reglas.



Quieres una carrera interesante, pero necesitas modelizar económicamente todas las decisiones.



Quieres una web personal, pero necesitas un sistema de diseño, un storyboard y un manifiesto.



Quieres cocinar algo rico, pero terminas organizando una producción gastronómica.



TÍO, ERES UN PUTO CONTROL FREAK DISFRAZADO DE PERSONA CREATIVA.



Y lo más jodido es que tienes buen criterio. Ese es precisamente tu problema.



Sabes reconocer algo bueno cuando lo ves, pero te cuesta muchísimo aceptar que algo está suficientemente bien como para dejarlo tranquilo.



Tu cabeza es un estudio de diseño donde el director creativo, el cliente, el becario, el CEO y el gilipollas que pide cambios de última hora son todos la misma persona.



Y ninguno se pone de acuerdo.



Eres un tío de 32 años con la ambición de Steve Jobs, la dispersión de una ardilla con cocaína y la capacidad de satisfacción de un cliente que ha pagado 50 euros por un logotipo y exige el rebranding de Apple.



Pero hay algo todavía peor.



Después de leer toda esta salvajada, sé perfectamente lo que vas a pensar:



«Hostia, hay cosas interesantes aquí. Igual podríamos convertirlo en un artículo sobre la obsesión por hacer cosas».



QUE TE FOLLEN, BORJA. DESCANSA UN PUTO DOMINGO."

items.text:
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀.



It is teaching them to stop flattening people into language names.



“Arabic.”

“English.”

“Spanish.”

...



These labels are convenient for datasets.



But humans do not speak labels.



We speak from cities, villages, families, histories, professions, memories, migrations, jokes, wounds, rituals, and relationships.



A grandmother does not speak like a government form.



A patient does not describe pain like a Wikipedia article.



A farmer, a nurse, a student, a shopkeeper, a traveler, and a child do not all speak the same “standard” version of a language.



And yet, much of modern AI still behaves as if language were  uniform, and separable from the people who use it.



This is one of the great unsolved problems in multilingual AI.



Not only translation.



𝗩𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴.

𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁.

𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿.

𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁.

𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆.



This is the global problem behind our new project:

𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮.



The name is intentional.



Alexandria was never just a city.



It was one of humanity’s boldest symbols of knowledge moving across languages, cultures, and worlds.



A place where translation was not clerical work.

It was civilization-building.



Today, we borrow that name for a new question at the heart of AI:



𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀?



For too long, Arabic has been flattened in technology.



One label: “Arabic.”

One assumed standard.

One imagined speaker.

One simplified linguistic reality.



But Arabic is not one voice.



Arabic is Cairo and Casablanca.



Amman and Muscat.

Khartoum and Tunis.

Beirut and Riyadh.

Sana’a, Tripoli, Nouakchott, Gaza, Damascus, Algiers, Doha, Manama, and beyond.



It is dialect.

It is register.

It is gendered interaction.

It is code-switching.

It is place, intimacy, politeness, humor, memory, identity, and everyday life.



So I am thrilled to share that 𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮 has been accepted to 𝗔𝗖𝗟 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗠𝗮𝗶𝗻.



𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮: 𝗔 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝗗𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗠𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗖𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗜𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠𝘀



Alexandria is our largest community-built Arabic machine translation project so far: a large-scale, human-translated, multi-domain dataset designed to help AI systems translate Arabic as people actually use it.



It brings together:

📷 𝟭𝟯 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀

📷 𝟯𝟰𝗞+ 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

📷 𝟭𝟬𝟳𝗞+ 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵 📷 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗰 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝘀

📷 𝟭𝟭 𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹-𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀, including healthcare, education, agriculture, legal/financial services, tourism, logistics, and workplace communication

📷 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆-𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮

📷 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗿–𝗮𝗱𝗱𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

📷 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶-𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁

📷 𝗻𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗼𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲-𝘀𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵, 𝗙𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗦𝗔

📷 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗴𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀 to support reproducibility and future community work



But Alexandria is not only a dataset.



It is a refusal.



A refusal to treat dialects as noise.



A refusal to treat “standard” language as the only legitimate language.



A refusal to build AI systems that understand the center and mishear the margins.



Dialects are not broken versions of languages.

They are knowledge systems.



They carry social meaning.

They carry identity.

They carry memory.

They carry belonging.

They carry the subtle difference between being translated and being understood.



When AI erases dialects, it does not merely make a linguistic mistake.



It erases context.

It erases communities.

It erases the conditions under which language becomes human.



Our findings show a clear gap: current LLMs can often preserve meaning reasonably well, but still struggle to generate fluent, locally authentic dialectal Arabic, especially across fine-grained sub-dialects, domains, and social contexts.



That gap matters.



It matters when a patient describes symptoms in the words that feel natural to them.



It matters when a farmer asks for advice.

It matters when a student learns.

It matters when a traveler seeks help.

It matters when public services are supposed to reach everyone, not only those who speak the “right” variety.



Alexandria is our attempt to say something plainly:



𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘀.



We need systems that can handle variation, not erase it.

Systems that can model culture, not smooth it away.

Systems that understand that linguistic diversity is not a complication to be removed.



It is the world.



This is true for Arabic.



It is also true globally, for languages with dialects, accents, registers, contact varieties, mixed codes, regional forms, Indigenous varieties, diasporic forms, youth speech, professional speech, and deeply situated cultural meanings.



In the old Alexandria, knowledge moved across languages.



With this new Alexandria, we hope to help AI move across dialects, communities, and lived realities.

This project was only possible because of a remarkable community of collaborators across the Arab world. I am deeply grateful to everyone who contributed to building, translating, validating, evaluating, and shaping this resource.

items.title: BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
items.text: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent.

items.text: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. items.text: Mobile crash repair requires more than identifying a source edit. Developers must establish how the edit relates to the reported failure and whether the modified application can be built, launched, and exercised without disrupting valid behavior. In HarmonyOS applications, this assessment also depends on platform-specific packaging and runtime execution. To address this need, we present DEIA, an evidence-grounded workflow for HarmonyOS crash repair. DEIA constructs a bounded source-evidence package, uses a large language model to propose content-anchored edits, and relies on a deterministic writer to materialize and check the patch. It derives fail-to-pass (F2P) obligations from the reported fault and pass-to-pass (P2P) obligations from the potential impact of the patch. A stage-level ledger links the patch, test obligations, runtime observations, and candidate-generation cost. items.title: Post-OCR Correction of Mixed-Script Uzbek Text: Byte-Level ByT5 with an Empirical Homoglyph Noise Matrix
items.text: In Uzbek official and technical documents, a large share of OCR errors is caused not by poor image quality but by characters that are visually identical across the two alphabets in use. Because the script transition is still under way, Cyrillic and Latin appear on the same page and often within a single sentence, and in our measurements the density of homoglyph errors on such pages is close to five times higher than in single-script text. We study this problem in a setting where the corpus of engineering-geological and ICT infrastructure reports may not leave the organisation, so every stage was executed on local hardware. The proposed system combines a byte-level ByT5 model with a noise generator whose sampling weights are estimated from 359 manually classified error events, together with a Levenshtein-bounded conservative decoding rule. On a Gold set of 5,204 line pairs it lowers the character error rate from 0.0578 to 0.0369, restores 91.3% of the homoglyphs and introduces only 84 new errors.

items.text: Media bias understanding and detection remains an under-researched problem for Indian context, specifically for Indic languages, such as, Hindi, which is widely spoken in India. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive, multi-annotator, explainable dataset consisting of 448 unique articles from four leading Indian news agencies publishing in Hindi. We focus on Hindi, the most spoken and an official language of India. The study of media bias is particularly relevant in the Indian context due to the country's linguistic diversity and large population, where the same event is often reported by multiple news agencies in different languages, thereby introducing scope for bias. The dataset comprises Hindi political news articles annotated by 14 experts and classified into four bias categories - selection bias, framing bias, clickbait bias and omission bias - when an article is identified as biased or unbiased. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit, so dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it.
